questions.q: Why does the lesson treat production monitoring as a research input rather than purely an operations concern?
options: Because operations teams are not capable of reading dashboards
Because a model being quietly wrong due to input distribution shift is a research problem -- the model or approach needs rework, and only instrumented production traffic reveals that
Because research teams are responsible for all server uptime
Because operations concerns and research concerns are identical by definition
questions.explain: A held-out eval score only describes performance against the training-time distribution. If production drifts away from that distribution, the fix is a research problem (new data, new approach), not an infrastructure fix -- so production needs to surface that signal.

questions.q: What does the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test compare in the drift-detection example?
options: Two different model architectures' accuracy scores
A feature's distribution in a recent production window against its distribution in the original training set
The latency of two different serving frameworks
Two versions of the same git commit
questions.explain: ks_2samp is run on a feature's training-time values against recent production values, producing a p-value for whether the two distributions are statistically distinguishable.

questions.q: What is a 'hard examples' set, and what is it used for?
options: A list of the most difficult unit tests in the codebase
A growing collection of low-confidence or flagged-incorrect production predictions, periodically reviewed and folded into the next training run's eval set
The set of production servers with the highest CPU load
A benchmark dataset published by the original paper's authors
questions.explain: Hard examples are logged from production (low confidence or user-flagged) and reviewed by the research team, with representative ones added to the eval set for the next research cycle.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what should actually trigger escalating a monitoring signal into a new research backlog item?
options: Any single drift alert, no matter how brief
A sustained signal -- a drift p-value below threshold across several consecutive windows, or an error rate meaningfully above the original baseline, not one noisy reading
A fixed weekly schedule regardless of what monitoring shows
Whenever a user complains on social media
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes routine eval-set accumulation from an actual research escalation: escalation requires a sustained, consistent signal, not a single noisy drift reading.

questions.q: How does closing the production-to-research loop connect to Lesson 40's eval harness and manifest practices?
options: It replaces the eval harness entirely with live monitoring dashboards
It extends the same eval harness and baseline score to incorporate newly discovered hard examples, so the next research cycle starts from an eval set that reflects what production actually saw
It has no connection; monitoring and eval harnesses are unrelated practices
It requires deleting the original production manifest before each new research cycle
questions.explain: The hard-examples review feeds into the same eval set infrastructure from Lesson 40, so the next research cycle's eval harness reflects real production blind spots instead of only the original training-time distribution.
